title: ‘You saw it all and let it go’
theme: Death praises Naciketas: he saw the fulfilment of desire, the support of the world, the endless reward of the rite, the far shore of fearlessness, the great and praised, the wide-reaching, the abiding — and, steady and wise, let it all go.

words.context: Śaṅkara: «समाप्तिम्», where all desires are fulfilled

words.gram: adj. used as noun, n. acc. sg.

words.context: Śaṅkara: «विस्तीर्णां गतिम्»; Madhva: a name of the Lord

sandhi.rule: Like vowels join long, P. 6.1.101 (अकः सवर्णे दीर्घः). GRETIL writes kāmasya āptiṃ with the vowels apart (corrections.json; orthographic).
The final s of kratoḥ (P. 8.2.66 (ससजुषो रुँः)) is r before a vowel after o.
stomamahat before u becomes stomamahad, P. 8.2.39 (झलां जशोऽन्ते).

sandhi.type: aḥ before a voiced consonant; aḥ before a
sandhi.rule: dhīraḥ before n becomes dhīro, P. 6.1.114 (हशि च) and P. 6.1.87 (आद्गुणः). naciketaḥ before a becomes naciketo and the a is elided (avagraha), P. 6.1.113 (अतो रोरप्लुतादप्लुते), P. 6.1.87 (आद्गुणः), P. 6.1.109 (एङः पदान्तादति).

samasa.meaning: praiseworthy and great; Raṅgarāmānuja’s text writes stomaṃ mahad, Madhva reads ‘greater than praises’ (see ambiguities)
wide going, far-reaching — Śaṅkara: «विस्तीर्णां गतिम्»; Madhva takes it as a name of the Lord

morphology.note: Abstract noun from ananta ‘endless’ with -ya. The regular form lengthens the first vowel, ānantyam, which the vishvAsa mūla, Madhva’s text and Raṅgarāmānuja read and which Śaṅkara gives as his gloss: «अनन्त्यम् आनन्त्यम्». The syllable count is the same either way.
Sigmatic aorist of ati-√sṛj with the augment a-, 2nd sg.: ‘you have released, passed over’. The same verb closes 1.2.3.
Used twice. Śaṅkara takes the first as the support of the world («आश्रयं सर्वात्मकत्वात्») and the second as one’s own unsurpassed abiding («स्थितिमात्मनोऽनुत्तमामपि»).

translation.literal: Having seen the attainment of desire, the support of the world, the endlessness of the rite, the far shore of fearlessness, the praiseworthy-great, the wide-going, the abiding, you, wise [one], O Naciketas, with steadfastness have let [them] go.
translation.readable: You saw the fulfilment of every desire, the ground on which the world stands, the endless reward of ritual, the far shore where there is no fear, a station great and praised, wide-reaching and secure — and, Naciketas, wise and steady, you let it all go.

anvaya: नचिकेतः, [त्वम्] कामस्य आप्तिम्, जगतः प्रतिष्ठाम्, क्रतोः अनन्त्यम्, अभयस्य पारम्, स्तोममहत्, उरुगायम्, प्रतिष्ठाम् [च] दृष्ट्वा धीरः [सन्] धृत्या अत्यस्राक्षीः ।
syntax: One sentence. A series of accusatives, not joined by ca, depends on the absolutive dṛṣṭvā ‘having seen’; then come the manner (dhṛtyā), the predicate adjective dhīraḥ, the vocative and the main verb atyasrākṣīḥ. How many things the list names, and whether it describes one goal or several, the verse leaves open.

ambiguities.note: Śaṅkara: the whole list describes Hiraṇyagarbha’s station, the highest fruit of meditation — «क्रतोः उपासनायाः फलं हैरण्यगर्भं पदम्» — which the boy saw and still gave up. Raṅgarāmānuja gives two readings: the first items are the fruit of rites and the later ones describe liberation; or the whole list is said of the supreme Self — «सर्वं परमात्मविषयतया योजनीयम्». Madhva: the boy saw Urugāya, the Lord, and let go of the attainment of desires — «उरुगायं दृष्ट्वा कामस्याप्तिमत्यस्राक्षीः».

Śaṅkara: one compound, ‘praiseworthy and great’ — «स्तोमं च तन्महच्च निरतिशयत्वात् स्तोममहत्». Raṅgarāmānuja’s text writes stomaṃ mahad, two words, and he takes stoma as the mass of great qualities, «अपहतपाप्मत्वसत्यसंकल्पत्वादिमहागुणगणरूपस्तोमं». Madhva: what even praises cannot wholly reach, greater than praises — «स्तोमैरपि सर्वात्मना प्राप्तुमशक्यम् । स्तोमेभ्योऽपि महान्तम्».

metre.name: triṣṭubh
metre.note: Triṣṭubh, 21 + 24 syllables: pādas of 10, 11, 11 and 13. As joined, the first pāda (kāmasyāptiṃ jagataḥ pratiṣṭhāṃ) has ten; GRETIL’s kāmasya āptiṃ, with the vowels apart, counts eleven. The last pāda (dṛṣṭvā dhṛtyā dhīro naciketo ’tyasrākṣīḥ) has thirteen in every witness. ānantyam for anantyam does not change the count.

beginner: Death now praises the boy. He lists what Naciketas has been shown: the fulfilment of every wish, the ground the whole world stands on, the endless reward that rituals promise, a far shore where there is no fear, a high and praised position that reaches far and stays secure. And Naciketas, steady and wise, let all of it go. The list is deliberately grand. Śaṅkara reads it as the highest heaven a person can reach by meditation, the station of the cosmic Creator, and says the boy refused even that because he wanted only the highest. Raṅgarāmānuja offers two readings, in one of which the later words describe liberation itself. Madhva says the boy saw the Lord, and so gave up the rest. In every reading the praise is for one thing: the boy could see something magnificent and still say, not this.
analogy: Like a student offered the directorship of a famous institute who turns it down because it is not the question they came to ask.

commentary.label: direct
commentary.text: Naciketas saw a series of great things — the attainment of desire, the support of the world, the endless fruit of the rite, the far shore of fearlessness, a great, wide-reaching and abiding station — and with steadfastness let them go.

commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Śaṅkara reads the list as the highest fruit of meditation, where every desire is fulfilled — «अत्र हि सर्वे कामाः परिसमाप्ताः» — the fruit of the rite being Hiraṇyagarbha’s station, «क्रतोः उपासनायाः फलं हैरण्यगर्भं पदम्». Naciketas, wanting only the highest, gave up the whole range of worldly enjoyment: «परमेवाकाङ्क्षन्नतिसृष्टवानसि सर्वमेतत्संसारभोगजातम्».

commentary.q: Raṅgarāmānuja: why the boy may hear
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Raṅgarāmānuja takes the verse as unfolding the wish at the close of 1.2.9 for a questioner like Naciketas: it shows his fitness to hear — «पूर्वमन्त्रोक्तं नचिकेतसः श्रवणाधिकारं विवृणोति». The boy saw the fruit of rites and the greatness of liberation, and in his wisdom gave up worldly desires: «लौकिकान् कामान् प्रज्ञाशालित्वात् त्यक्तवानसि इत्यर्थः». Or the whole list describes the supreme Self: «सर्वं परमात्मविषयतया योजनीयम्».

commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Madhva takes urugāya as the Lord’s name, and concludes that Naciketas’ question is not about the individual soul: «उरुगायमित्युक्तत्वाच्च न जीवविषयोऽयं प्रश्नः». Having seen Urugāya, the boy let go of the attainment of desires — «उरुगायं दृष्ट्वा कामस्याप्तिमत्यस्राक्षीः». He adds that a boy who had died and come to Yama could not be asking whether the dead exist: «न च मृत्वा यमं प्राप्तस्य नचिकेतसो मृतोऽस्ति न वेति संशयो युज्यते».

commentary.label: linguistic
commentary.text: AS and GRETIL read anantyam; the vishvAsa mūla, Madhva’s text and Raṅgarāmānuja read ānantyam, the regular abstract, which Śaṅkara supplies as his gloss: «अनन्त्यम् आनन्त्यम्». The sense, ‘endlessness’, is the same (corrections.json).

advaita.text: The list describes Hiraṇyagarbha’s station, the summit of what meditation can win; Naciketas rejected even that for the highest: «परमेवाकाङ्क्षन्नतिसृष्टवानसि सर्वमेतत्संसारभोगजातम्».

visistadvaita.text: Two readings: worldly fruit set against the greatness of liberation, or the whole list said of the supreme Self — «सर्वं परमात्मविषयतया योजनीयम्». Either way the verse shows the boy fit to hear.

dvaita.text: The boy saw Urugāya, the Lord: «उरुगायं दृष्ट्वा कामस्याप्तिमत्यस्राक्षीः». The word urugāya shows that the question concerns the Lord, not the soul.

schools.disagreement: For Śaṅkara the whole list is what was given up; for Madhva its key word names what was seen; Raṅgarāmānuja allows both. All three praise the same renunciation.

parallels.note: The Kaṭha returns to ‘the far shore of fearlessness’ in 1.3.2; Madhva cites that verse in his comment here.
Madhva quotes this half-line in his comment on the verse, among passages he reads as stating difference: the self is the arrow, Brahman its target.

contemporary.text: Turning down a small temptation is easy to admire. Turning down a magnificent and legitimate prize — real influence, deserved praise — is harder to recognise as wisdom, because it can look like a lack of ambition. The verse praises exactly this: seeing something great clearly and still deciding it is not what one is looking for. This is a reflection, not a claim made by the text.

reflect.beginner: Have you ever said no to something good because it was not what you were looking for?
reflect.deeper: Why might the verse list the greatest prizes rather than obvious vices? What does refusal mean when what is refused is genuinely good?
reflect.practice: Name one good thing you pursue mainly because others admire it. Ask whether you would still want it if no one knew.

flags.note: anantyam (AS, GRETIL) or ānantyam (vishvAsa mūla, Madhva’s text, Raṅgarāmānuja); Śaṅkara glosses with ānantyam (corrections.json).
stomamahat: one compound (Śaṅkara), stomaṃ mahad (Raṅgarāmānuja’s text), or ‘greater than praises’ (Madhva).
